title: Five Principles of Effective Modelling
author: Didau, David
summary: Modeling is essential for teaching but often done poorly. Single exemplars don't work, overly polished models discourage students, and direct copying replaces understanding. Didau outlines five principles for effective modeling: comparison clarifies quality, model structure not content, surface problems before solutions, use narration to direct attention, and gradually release responsibility. Good models reduce cognitive load for novices but become counterproductive for growing experts (expertise reversal effect).
points: Comparison clarifies quality far better than judging a single example against abstract standards.
Model the structure and thinking process, not content that students will copy verbatim.
Surface problems and common misconceptions before showing polished solutions.
Narration and think-aloud commentary direct students to notice what matters.
As students gain expertise, models become unhelpful; gradually release responsibility instead.
quotes: When students are new to a domain, problem solving extracts a heavy toll on working memory.
All judgments are comparisons of one thing with another.
Instead of having to judge one response against an abstract standard, students can inspect two responses side by side.
If modelling is to be effective, it must sharpen judgement, direct attention, reveal process, and help students see what is and is not important.
What supports a beginner can become unhelpfully constraining for someone more fluent.” Archived from David Didau Blog on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
